intro: The AI world is reeling today as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy sent the chipmaker's stock tumbling and raised urgent questions about the security of America's most critical AI infrastructure. But the industry isn't standing still — Google DeepMind is making Gemini 4 Carbon widely available, OpenAI is turning ChatGPT into a storefront with verified Business Agents, and a staggering 181GW of gas-fired power plants are being planned just to keep AI's lights on. It's a day that captures the full spectrum of AI's current moment: geopolitical risk, fierce competition, and an energy appetite that's reshaping the grid.

stories.title: Nvidia in crisis after Jensen Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy
stories.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Nvidia's stock dropped roughly 9.5% over two days. The board has hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation. Key questions center on what information Alice Huang may have obtained and when Jensen Huang became aware of espionage suspicions. Experts warn that failing to inform the board could be a fireable offense, and shareholder lawsuits including securities fraud claims are expected. The incident threatens US AI leadership given Nvidia's critical role as the dominant designer of advanced AI chips, with major companies like Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI dependent on its products. The board has stated it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
stories.opinion: A genuine national security crisis masquerading as a corporate governance scandal. Nvidia's near-monopoly on advanced AI chips makes this far more consequential than a typical CEO misconduct story — the fragility of the US AI lead is now uncomfortably visible. Where coverage differs: TechCrunch focuses on corporate governance precedent, shareholder lawsuits, and board response; The Verge emphasizes national security implications and the fragility of the US AI lead over China

sources.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn

conflicts: TechCrunch focuses on corporate governance precedent, shareholder lawsuits, and board response; The Verge emphasizes national security implications and the fragility of the US AI lead over China
cluster.reason: Both cover the Nvidia scandal involving CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, the resulting stock drop, and national security concerns.

stories.title: OpenAI launches verified Business Agents in ChatGPT
stories.summary: OpenAI launched 'Business Agents' in ChatGPT, a beta feature allowing US e-commerce and online service brands to claim verified profiles, monitor how often ChatGPT mentions them, and deploy AI agents that interact directly with users for tasks like comparison shopping. A 'Business Hub' lets companies configure agent instructions, add product details, and view analytics on brand mentions and click-throughs. Chats with Business Agents are clearly labeled and separated from main conversations. Brands can also pay to make their agent the landing page for ChatGPT ads. The feature is currently free to claim.
stories.opinion: A significant move to monetize ChatGPT's massive user base by turning it into a commerce platform. The separation of brand chats from regular conversations is wise, but the paid placement option raises questions about whether ChatGPT recommendations will remain impartial. Where coverage differs: The Rundown AI reports brands can pay to make their agent the landing page for ChatGPT ads; The Verge does not mention this paid placement option

OpenAI invites brands to set up shop in ChatGPT

conflicts: The Rundown AI reports brands can pay to make their agent the landing page for ChatGPT ads; The Verge does not mention this paid placement option
cluster.reason: Both describe OpenAI's launch of verified Business Agents in ChatGPT, allowing brands to claim profiles and deploy AI agents for customer interactions.

stories.title: Adobe shows experimental AI features at MAX 2026 including character interviews and 3D photo exploration
stories.summary: Adobe showcased experimental AI features at MAX 2026, including Project Screen Test, which lets users design AI characters by conversing with them in an audition-like environment to define personality traits, voice, backstory, and quirks through natural conversation. Other experiments include a tool that transforms 2D images into explorable 3D scenes and a feature that simplifies photo editing into a copy/paste process.
stories.opinion: Project Screen Test is the standout — defining characters through conversation rather than text prompts is a genuinely novel interaction pattern that could reshape creative workflows if it graduates from experiment to product.

sources.title: Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters

cluster.reason: Covers additional experimental AI features shown at Adobe's MAX 2026 conference, the same event as yesterday's Adobe coverage.

stories.title: Google DeepMind makes Gemini 4 Carbon generally available
stories.summary: Google DeepMind announced the general availability of Gemini 4 Carbon on November 10, 2026. Carbon is positioned as their strongest frontier model, with leading performance in cybersecurity, long-horizon agentic workflows, complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. It was initially released to cybersecurity defenders via Google's Fairwind Program two weeks prior. Carbon complements the earlier Gemini 4 Argon model — Argon is recommended for most software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon targets tasks at the limits of model intelligence such as complex multi-step coding/debugging and open-ended scientific research.
stories.opinion: The cybersecurity-first rollout via the Fairwind Program was a smart trust-building move. The Argon/Carbon split mirrors Anthropic's Sonnet/Opus tiering — the frontier AI market is converging on a 'good enough for most tasks' plus 'maximum capability' product structure.

stories.title: AI datacenter developers planning 181GW of on-site gas-fired power stations
stories.summary: Research reveals that AI datacenter developers across the US, UK, and mainland Europe are planning to build on-site gas-fired power stations totaling 181GW of capacity. This massive buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure is being driven by delays in connecting datacenters to national electricity grids, as the rapid expansion of AI computing demands more power than existing grid connections can supply.
stories.opinion: 181GW is a staggering figure — roughly equivalent to the entire installed electricity generation capacity of the UK. This undermines the clean energy commitments many tech companies have made and suggests the AI boom's environmental costs are being systematically underestimated.

stories.title: Math educator builds family knowledge system with Claude Code and Obsidian
stories.summary: Scott Farrar, a math educator and parent, built a household knowledge management system using Claude Code and Obsidian. The system uses Markdown files to track appliances, warranties, insurance documents, and family to-do lists, with a DAKboard wall display showing priority tasks. He demonstrates using it to shop for car insurance and plan home repairs. The conversation also covers AI in math education, where Farrar advocates for a 'flipped tutor' approach that keeps students doing the thinking rather than letting AI do it for them.
stories.opinion: A practical, relatable use case that shows Claude Code's utility beyond software development. The 'flipped tutor' idea for math education — making AI support student thinking rather than replace it — is a valuable pedagogical insight.

stories.title: Plurai raises $13M to improve AI agent reliability using autonomous driving simulation techniques
stories.summary: Plurai, founded by former Nexar employees who worked on autonomous driving technology, raised $13 million in seed funding to improve AI agent reliability. The company creates digital twins of corporate electronic systems, maps all possible agent workflows, and uses synthetic data to evaluate and fix edge cases. Their key value proposition is post-training smaller, open-weight models tailored to individual customers, claiming to match or exceed frontier model quality at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer.
stories.opinion: The autonomous driving simulation analogy is compelling — systematically testing edge cases before deployment is exactly what enterprise AI agents need. The claim of matching frontier model quality at 1-2 orders of magnitude lower cost deserves scrutiny but would be transformative if true.

stories.title: OpenAI acquires AI travel startup Odessia in apparent acqui-hire
stories.summary: OpenAI acquired Odessia, a year-old AI travel agent startup founded by Francis Davidson, the well-known founder of Sonder. The deal appears to be an acqui-hire, with Davidson now working at OpenAI on travel-related initiatives. Odessia had raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and helped users plan millions of dollars worth of travel before being shut down. Travel is a frequent use case among ChatGPT's 1.2 billion weekly users, and OpenAI already partners with Booking.com, Expedia, and KAYAK.
stories.opinion: With 1.2 billion weekly users frequently asking about travel, building native travel capabilities makes obvious commercial sense. The acqui-hire of a Sequoia-backed founder signals OpenAI is serious about vertical commerce, not just horizontal AI.

stories.title: Editorial cartoon laments Australians not streaming local music, blames AI algorithms
stories.summary: An editorial cartoon by First Dog on the Moon in The Guardian laments that Australians are not streaming Australian music. The cartoonist suggests the likely reasons are that live music has become too expensive and difficult to attend, and that AI-driven streaming algorithms are shaping and narrowing listeners' habits, steering them away from local artists.
stories.opinion: A lightweight cultural commentary, but the underlying point about AI recommendation algorithms homogenizing music discovery and disadvantaging local artists is a real concern shared by music industries worldwide.

stories.title: Guardian podcast revisits ELIZA creator Joseph Weizenbaum's turn against AI
stories.summary: A Guardian podcast revisits a 2023 article about Joseph Weizenbaum, the MIT computer scientist who created ELIZA in 1966. Weizenbaum was disturbed when users formed genuine emotional attachments to the program despite knowing it was just software. This experience, combined with observations of how computers were being applied to military and surveillance systems during the Cold War, led him to become one of AI's most prominent internal critics. His 1976 book 'Computer Power and Human Reason' argued that there are tasks computers should never be entrusted with — not because they can't perform them, but because doing so undermines human judgment and responsibility.
stories.opinion: Weizenbaum's core argument — that capability is not the same as appropriateness — feels more relevant than ever in the age of frontier AI models. A timely archival piece given current debates about AI agent autonomy and emotional attachment to chatbots.

tweet_headlines.author: mattpocockuk
tweet_headlines.headline: Matt Pocock's __home repo pattern__ lets you run agents across multiple codebases from a single place — simpler than it sounds, reportedly viral in his course.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
A lot of folks ask me "how do you work with agents in multiple repos at once?"

I have a very simple solution - the Home Repo

I have a single repo (the home) where all of my skills, steering files, wiki etc live.

I run my agent in the home repo, and then inside AGENTS.md I have pointers to the other repos:

```
For skills, clone mattpocock/skills to ~/repos/skills.
For Sandcastle, clone mattpocock/sandcastle to ~/repos/sandcastle
```

This is extremely simple and incredibly effective. The home repo lets you:

1. Put all your steering files and tooling in one place
2. Have a single spot to run all your agents in
3. Make sweeping changes over multiple repos

Talked about this in the course yesterday and folks are loving it (see below).

I'm sure you will too. Enjoy!

tweet_headlines.author: jianw851
tweet_headlines.headline: One engineer argues software just moved to an __Agent-Driven Lifecycle (ADLC)__ — agents writing, testing, and deploying in parallel while requirements evolve in real time.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
AI agent–enabled coding is quietly becoming the new SDLC.

Software development just had its biggest shift since the GUI.

Planning.
Coding.
Testing.
Deployment.

Agents are starting to handle all of it.

Here’s the shift most engineers haven’t noticed yet 👇

Old model: SDLC

• sequential phases
• human-driven execution
• testing happens after development
• changing requirements break timelines

Everything moves step → by → step.

New model: ADLC (Agent-Driven Lifecycle)

• agents write, refactor, and test code
• multiple tasks run in parallel
• requirements evolve dynamically
• feedback loops happen in real time

Instead of a pipeline…

You get a live development system.

6 major shifts happening right now

1️⃣ Driver
Human execution → Autonomous agents

2️⃣ Planning
Fixed scope → Evolving goals & PRDs

3️⃣ Development Speed
Sequential handoffs → Parallel sub-agents

4️⃣ Testing
Post-development QA → Continuous testing

5️⃣ Adaptability
Mid-cycle chaos → Real-time re-planning

6️⃣ Feedback Loop
End-of-project retros → Live monitoring

Some early signals are already here.

According to agentic coding reports:

• teams at Wiz and CRED doubled execution speed
• large-scale repos are being modified autonomously
• complex implementations completed in hours instead of days

How engineers should adapt

1️⃣ Start with one agent
Automate testing first.

2️⃣ Learn to write clear PRDs
Agents execute exactly what you define.

3️⃣ Introduce parallel sub-agents
Break one large task into smaller workstreams.

4️⃣ Review outcomes, not every line of code

5️⃣ Build live feedback loops
Agents should detect issues before you do.

The future of software development isn’t just faster coding.

It’s agent-driven systems building software.

#AI #AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering #SDLC #GenAI #AIEngineering

tweet_headlines.author: moritzkremb
tweet_headlines.headline: Moritz Kremb breaks down Anthropic's __Fable 5.2 prompting guide__: calibrate effort per task, add a "finish the work" block, and always tell it who owns the code.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Anthropic just released a prompting guide for Claude Fable 5.2.

Here are the 10 rules:

1. Switching effort per task matters more than ever. Fable 5.2 decides on its own how much to think, and effort is now the main way to control it. Low is strong on this model, and going above high mostly costs more tokens.

2. Delete your "don't overthink" lines. On medium and above, they don't stop it from thinking. Lower the effort instead.

3. Tell it to finish. On long tasks it can stop early and hand you a to-do list. Add a short "finish the work" block to your instructions.

4. Say who owns the code. Otherwise it tends to copy code instead of cleaning it up, and reports nearby bugs instead of fixing them.

5. Keep your "never" rules narrow. It follows them very literally, so vague warnings make it ask permission for normal stuff.

6. Ask for progress updates. Otherwise it can go quiet for a lot of tool calls in a row.

7. Put limits on helper agents. Sub-agents can be a big part of what a session costs.

8. Ask for reports that make sense on their own. Key points first, plain words, no made-up labels.

9. Don't ask it to show its internal thinking. Requests to paste its reasoning get refused. "Explain your reasoning" is fine.

10. Loosen hard style rules. Caps like "20 words per sentence" make its writing choppy.

Overall, treat Fable 5.2 like a senior colleague. It's smart and takes everything you say seriously, so old rules and workarounds mostly get in its way. Pick the right effort, clean out the old stuff, and give it room to make its own calls.

Full guide here:
https://t.co/NKtkUc8EFC

tweet_headlines.source_text:
how to audit your Claude sessions with Fable 5.2 (and 10x your AI productivity)

map out how you work across all your Claude projects, then let Fable optimize it

you´ll get new skills, workflows to automate and a cleaner workspace

Step by step guide (save this):

1. find your sessions

Claude Code saves every session on your machine, one folder per project in ~/.claude/projects, and ~/.claude/history.jsonl holds every prompt you typed

it deletes sessions older than 30 days by default, so raise cleanupPeriodDays in ~/.claude/settings.json to give your next audit more history

2. map how you work

the sessions are plain text and can hold keys from .env files, so ask Fable to leave secrets out of the map

then give it the projects folder and history.jsonl, and ask it to map:

> the prompts you type again and again
> the corrections you keep giving
> the tasks you still do by hand
> the sessions that stall or loop
> the skills and rules you never use

3. let Fable optimize it

ask for one plan that turns the map into:

> new skills for the prompts you repeat
> workflows and hooks for the tasks you do by hand
> AGENTS .md rules for the corrections you keep giving
> a cleaner workspace, with old projects, unused skills and stale instructions archived

4. review the plan before any file changes

then hand it to Opus or GPT to build, and have Fable review the result

human_items.headline: Plurai raises $13M to improve AI agent reliability using autonomous driving simulation techniques
human_items.summary: Plurai, founded by former Nexar employees who worked on autonomous driving technology, raised $13 million in seed funding to improve AI agent reliability. The company creates digital twins of corporate electronic systems, maps all possible agent workflows, and uses synthetic data to evaluate and fix edge cases. Their key value proposition is post-training smaller, open-weight models tailored to individual customers, claiming to match or exceed frontier model quality at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.

human_items.headline: Guardian podcast revisits ELIZA creator Joseph Weizenbaum's turn against AI
human_items.summary: A Guardian podcast revisits a 2023 article about Joseph Weizenbaum, the MIT computer scientist who created ELIZA in 1966. Weizenbaum was disturbed when users formed genuine emotional attachments to the program despite knowing it was just software. This experience, combined with observations of how computers were being applied to military and surveillance systems during the Cold War, led him to become one of AI's most prominent internal critics. His 1976 book 'Computer Power and Human Reason' argued that there are tasks computers should never be entrusted with — not because they can't perform them, but because doing so undermines human judgment and responsibility.
human_items.meaning: Decide the boundary before the tool is in daily use.
